question:
Three triangles and a diamond balance nine dots. Also, one triangle balances a diamond and a dot. How many dots will balance two diamonds?

[Figure 1](figures/1990_AMC_8_Q24_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The second balance tells us that a triangle can be replaced by a diamond and a dot without changing the weight. Replace all three triangles in the first balance this way. Its left side then contains four diamonds and three dots, which together balance nine dots.

Remove three dots from each side. Four diamonds therefore balance \(9-3=6\) dots. Taking half of each side shows that two diamonds balance \(6\div2=3\) dots. The answer is \(\boxed{3}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

reference.solution:
Method 1: Replace triangles with equal weights

The second balance tells us that a triangle can be replaced by a diamond and a dot without changing the weight. Replace all three triangles in the first balance this way. Its left side then contains four diamonds and three dots, which together balance nine dots.

Remove three dots from each side. Four diamonds therefore balance \(9-3=6\) dots. Taking half of each side shows that two diamonds balance \(6\div2=3\) dots. The answer is \(\boxed{3}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

Substituting an expression into a coefficient-bearing term can create a bracket that must be expanded with the correct sign.

Substitution seeks a pair satisfying both equations, so system and common-solution meanings are essential.
Substitution introduces the reduction-to-one-variable idea, but adding equations to cancel an unknown is justified independently by equality operations.
The reduction and back-substitution leave one-variable linear equations that must be solved; this is not a claim that every route must name transposition.
Adding/subtracting equations is performed to find their common solutions, not unrelated separate equation values.
